newsitem.title: NORWAY: New technology keeps Norway afloat in black gold.
newsitem.headline: New technology keeps Norway afloat in black gold.

text.p: State of the art technology has helped make Norway the world's second largest oil exporter, topping even the most optimistic forecasts of how much crude can be pumped from its offshore fields.
Just 10 years after forecasters predicted Norwegian oil production to be around 1 million barrels per day (bpd) by the mid-1990s, Norway pumps more than three times the amount.
Oil companies say innovative techniques may mean they will be able to again buck the trend of slowing output in the mature North Sea.
Norway pumps about 3.2 million barrels a day of oil to stand just behind Saudi Arabia among the world's top oil sellers. It uses 150,000 barrels a day of its oil at home.
"We were very wrong when we predicted (oil) volumes 10 years ago, wrong by a ratio of one-to-three," Energy Minister Jens Stoltenberg said recently.
"We are getting much more out of developed fields... A technological revolution has been seen on the Norwegian Continental Shelf (NCS)."
Much of the revolution has been driven by a move into the hostile deep waters of frontier acreage.
Norway's first oilfield, the Phillips-operated Ekofisk development, was developed in 1971 in just 70 meters (230 feet) of water.

In 1993, Royal Dutch Shell opened the taps on the Draugen field, lying in water depths of 240-270 meters (790-890 feet) and three years later Norway's own oil giant Statoil developed the Heidrun discovery at 350 meters (1,150 feet).
Today British Petroleum has plans for an exploration well in 1,350 meters (4,430 feet) of water on the Nyk High license in the Norwegian Sea.
More recently, as discoveries have become smaller, companies focus on adding value to existing developments.

"In the last five years industry has added about 2.5 billion barrels of extra recoverable oil due to improved recovery rates," said Arild Nystad, director of petroleum resource management at the Norwegian Petroleum Directorate (NPD).
"That has lifted the average recovery rate on the (Norwegian Continental Shelf) from 34 percent to 41 percent. We think it is realistic to expect average recovery to rise to about 47 percent."

Developments in reservoir mapping and drilling technology, together with industry-wide cooperation between operators, engineers and contractors is resulting in more cost-effective and efficient ways of boosting production.

"There are a lot of joint projects and there is a lot of cross fertilisation among the industry," said Arne Liverud, project director for Norsk Hydro. "Technology today is open, it's no secret. The key is how you implement it and get the most out of it."
Following an 18-month study on the Norwegian Continental Shelf, Statoil believes it will be possible to tap another 4.4 billion barrels of oil from 40 old and new finds between 1997 and 2016.

The plans call for gas-based injection methods and advanced wells such as branching wells and four-dimensional seismic mapping to capture the oil -- using time as the fourth dimension to analyse reservoir movements.
Adolfo Henriquez, Statoil chief engineer for reservoir engineering, says a better information and understanding of reservoir geology has led to many advances.
"Dual purpose wells for gas injection mean that we can now inject gas and at the same time produce from another part of the well. That was science fiction five years ago."
Drilling technology has made leaps and bounds since horizontal drilling became the buzz-phrase in the early 1990s.

Horizontal wells allow a change of direction of the drill bit to bore down laterally as well as vertically to reach hitherto inaccessible parts of reservoirs and cutting back on the number of wells needed.

Statoil was the first operator to use horizontal wells on the Norwegian Continental Shelf at the Gullfaks South prospect. Since then the technology has evolved to allow wells up to 10,000 meters (33,000 feet) in length to be drilled directly from platforms.
"We have mastered horizontal wells and now we are going into multilateral (branching) wells which make it possible to find small pockets of oil at low cost," Hydro's Liverud said.
Saga Petroleum plans to raise output at Snorre by using coiled tubing drilling (CTD) to drill so-called branches from existing wells.

Arne Wyller Christensen, Saga's vice president for drilling and well technology, says that by drilling two lateral branches in opposite directions at an existing injection well, the injection rate will double and improve oil recovery at that well by seven million barrels over the field life.

"So if we invest 20 million crowns ($3.1 million) on that well we will net back more than 250 million crowns ($38.75 million)... That's a pretty good investment," Christensen said. The CTD project is expected to raise Snorre's recoverable reserves of 179 million cubic meters by 10 to 20 percent.
